Not medical adviceAlzheimer's Companion is an educational synthesis of published literature for study, patient understanding and family caregivers. It does not replace a clinician. Doses and guideline statements are reported as published, not as instructions for any individual.

Alzheimer's disease · animated companion

Alzheimer's Companion

Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. Here it is in moving pictures: watch a protein get cut the wrong way, follow tangles spreading through the brain, see the changes that begin many years before the first forgotten name, and look honestly at what the newest drugs do and do not achieve.

Schematic. Amyloid rises first, tau follows, and memory changes come last.

For students

Every module has an Exam hook box and a citation trail. Finish with flashcards, mnemonics and a quiz.

For patients and families

Look for the In plain words boxes. Bring questions to your own clinician: the app reports what guidelines and studies say, not what you should do.

How sure is each claim?

Research claims carry a label: Established Early evidence Hypothesis. Small numbers link to the Sources list.

Part 1 · The disease

What Alzheimer's is

Dementia is not one disease. It is a pattern of decline that several diseases can cause, and Alzheimer's disease is the most common of them. Press play to build the picture, then see how the odds change with age.

Schematic. Circle sizes are not to scale; the bars and dots are.

Age is the strongest risk factor

Show

Each figure is 1 person in 100. US figures, Alzheimer's Association 2025.

The numbers, and where sources disagree

Counts depend on who is counting, which year, and whether they mean all dementia or Alzheimer's alone. Each card names its source so the figures can be compared fairly.

Worldwide, now

57 million

people were living with dementia in 2021, over 60% of them in low- and middle-income countries, with nearly 10 million new cases each year. 515 A secondary analysis of GBD 2021 counted 9.84 million new cases and 1.95 million deaths in 2021. 528

These are counts for all dementia, not Alzheimer's alone.

Worldwide, forecast

152.8 million by 2050

GBD 2019 projected a rise from 57.4 million in 2019. The age-standardised rate stays almost flat, so the growth comes from more people reaching old age. Projected increases range from 53% in high-income Asia Pacific to 367% in north Africa and the Middle East. 192

Against that, age-specific incidence seems to be falling in high-income countries. In Framingham, 5-year incidence fell from 3.6 to 2.0 per 100 people between the late 1970s and early 2010s, but only among people with at least a high-school diploma. 449

WHO's 57 million (2021) and GBD's 57.4 million (2019) are different years and methods, not a contradiction.

United States

7.2 million

Americans aged 65 and older were living with Alzheimer's dementia in 2025, about 1 in 9. About 22% of people over 65 have mild cognitive impairment, and roughly 5 to 7 million may have MCI due to Alzheimer's, an estimate the report says needs refining. 2

Sources differ The 2025 report projects 13.8 million by 2060. An earlier census-based model reached the same 13.8 million by 2050, a decade sooner. 2,229

Costs

$384 billion

US payments in 2025 for health care, long-term care and hospice for people with Alzheimer's or other dementias. Medicare and Medicaid pay $246 billion (64%), and out-of-pocket spending is $97 billion (25%). Annual payments are projected to reach just under $1 trillion by 2050. The lifetime cost of care for one person was estimated at $405,262, about 70% of it borne by families. 2

Worldwide, WHO puts the cost at US$1.3 trillion in 2019, about half of it attributable to informal carers. 515

Unpaid care

19.2 billion hours

In 2024, 11.9 million US family members and other unpaid caregivers gave an estimated 19.2 billion hours of care, valued at $413.5 billion. That averages nearly 31 hours per caregiver per week. 2

Worldwide, women provide 70% of the care hours for people living with dementia. 515 See Living with dementia and caregiving.

Women and men

4.4 vs 2.8 million

Almost two-thirds of older Americans with Alzheimer's dementia are women: 12% of women and 10% of men aged 65 and over. At age 45 the lifetime risk was about 1 in 5 for women and 1 in 10 for men in Framingham data. 2 Globally GBD estimated 1.69 women for every man with dementia in 2019. 192

Debated Why?

  • Longevity. Women live longer, and age is the strongest risk factor. Most US incidence studies find no meaningful sex difference at any given age.
  • Survival bias. Men who survive to 65 tend to have healthier hearts and vessels.
  • Biology Hypothesis Hormonal or reproductive factors, or a possibly stronger effect of APOE e4 in women.
  • Social and gender factors. The report says more research is needed. 2

A review argues that symptoms, rates of decline and brain atrophy differ by sex, and that sex should be used to stratify research and care. 170

Survival after diagnosis

4 to 8 years

on average for people diagnosed at 65 or older, and some live 20 years. 2 Age at diagnosis matters most:

Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging, with no significant difference between men and women. 64 A review found median survival of 3.2 to 6.6 years from diagnosis, and 7 to 10 years from onset in most studies. 487

Causes of death

7th

Alzheimer's was the seventh-leading cause of death in the US in 2022, with 120,122 recorded deaths, up more than 142% since 2000. Death certificates often name pneumonia instead, so the true count is higher. 2 Worldwide, WHO ranks dementia seventh too. 515

Pneumonia is the most commonly identified immediate cause, and swallowing problems can lead to aspiration pneumonia. 2 In 524 autopsies of people with dementia, bronchopneumonia caused 38.4% of deaths and ischaemic heart disease 23.1%, against 2.8% bronchopneumonia in the general older population. 65 In nursing-home residents with advanced dementia, 41.1% developed pneumonia over 18 months, and 46.7% died within six months of it. 358

Exam hookUS prevalence by age band: 5.1% (65–74), 13.2% (75–84), 33.4% (85+). Median survival falls from 8.3 years if diagnosed at 65 to 3.4 at 90. Pneumonia is the most common immediate cause of death. 2,64

Part 1 · The disease

The brain that forgets

Tau tangles and amyloid plaques both spread through the brain in a fixed order, but not the same order. Step through the tangle stages, then switch to amyloid and compare where each one starts.

Map

Schematic outlines. Deep structures are dashed. Regions outside a scheme are left unshaded; that does not mean they are spared.

Why memory goes first

The first tangles form where the hippocampal memory circuit begins. Follow a signal around the loop, then watch which neurons are lost, in the order the studies report.

Schematic. Dots on the loop are signals; faded dashed cells are lost neurons. The MRI shapes compound the published yearly rates, for illustration.

Scoring a brain at autopsy: the ABC score

The 2012 NIA-AA guidelines rate three things and combine them into one level of Alzheimer's neuropathologic change. Choose a rating for each and read the result. 246,366

A · amyloid plaques (Thal phase)
B · tangles (Braak stage)
C · neuritic plaques (CERAD)
How the levels combine

Not, Low, Intermediate, High

A0 is always "Not". With B0 or B1 the level is at most "Low". "High" needs A3, B3 and C2 or C3 together. "Intermediate" or "High" is considered a sufficient explanation for dementia. 366

The guidelines recognise that Alzheimer's changes can be present without cognitive impairment, and they set protocols for common co-pathologies: Lewy body disease, vascular brain injury, hippocampal sclerosis and TDP-43 inclusions. 246,366

In plain wordsAfter death, a pathologist scores how much amyloid, how far the tangles have spread and how many damaged plaques there are. Together they say how likely Alzheimer's explains the dementia.
Exam hookA = Thal (amyloid), B = Braak (tangles), C = CERAD (neuritic plaques). A0 → Not. B0–1 → at most Low. High = A3 + B3 + C2–3.

Table after Montine 2012, Table 3. B0 and B1 share a column in the original.

How strong is the amyloid case?

Part 1 · The disease

Tau and the tangle

Tau is a normal protein that holds the tracks inside a nerve fibre together. In Alzheimer's it collects too much phosphate, lets go, and folds into tangles. Press play to watch it happen, then see how it spreads.

Schematic, not to scale. Real microtubules are hollow tubes; the ladder is a teaching picture.

Spreading from cell to cell

Schematic network. Each node stands for a region, each line for a connection.

Tau tracks memory better than amyloid

"Weak" and "strong" give the direction each source reports, not a measured coefficient. The only coefficient shown, r = 0.96, is Terry 1991.

Part 1 · The disease

Microglia and the lost synapse

Memory depends on synapses, the contact points between neurons. In Alzheimer's they are lost early, and the brain's own immune cells help remove them. Press play to watch a patch of tissue change, then try the two switches.

Scenario

Schematic, not to scale. The synapse count is illustrative; the two ticks on the bar are measured human values.

Synapses track memory best

In 1991 Robert Terry's group counted synapses, plaques and tangles in the brains of 15 people with Alzheimer's and 9 controls, and compared each with how the person had scored on cognitive testing. Switch the measure on the x-axis and watch the cloud change shape. 484

Plot cognition against

Points are schematic, drawn to show the pattern, not Terry's data. The r of 0.96 is the published value.

The other cells, and the other diseases

Established

Astrocytes react too

Activated microglia release IL-1α, TNF and C1q, which push astrocytes into a reactive state, named "A1" in 2017, that supports neurons less well. Such astrocytes were abundant in Alzheimer's brains. 312

Debated

But "A1" and "A2" are too simple

A 2021 consensus statement criticised binary astrocyte labels (A1 versus A2, good versus bad) as oversimplified, and recommended describing reactive astrocytes with several measures at once. 143

Established

Microglial genes carry risk

TREM2 R47H raised risk about 2.9-fold. Other rare variants in microglial genes point the same way: PLCG2 P522R is protective (odds ratio 0.68), ABI3 S209F (1.43) and TREM2 R62H (1.67) raise risk. 263,464 More in Genes and inheritance.

Association only

A leaky barrier, early

Breakdown of the blood–brain barrier in the hippocampus was found in people with early cognitive problems, whatever their amyloid and tau status. The authors propose it as an independent early marker; the study shows association, not cause. 375

Most brains with Alzheimer's have something else too

Alzheimer's rarely travels alone in older brains. Each figure below comes from a different group of people, so the percentages cannot be added or compared directly.

Exam hookMixed pathology is the rule in old age, not the exception. LATE (limbic TDP-43) causes an amnestic dementia that mimics Alzheimer's, staged amygdala, then hippocampus, then middle frontal gyrus. 378,453

Sleep and the "glymphatic" system

Mostly rodent · contested

The mouse findings

In mice, fluid enters the brain along spaces around arteries and leaves around veins. Deleting the astrocyte water channel AQP4 cut solute clearance by about 70%. Sleep widened the space between cells by about 60% and sped amyloid clearance, and sleep restriction increased plaques. 247,269,526

Contrary evidence

Other labs disagree

An independent group found transport in brain tissue fitted diffusion, not flow, and did not depend on AQP4. A 2024 mouse study found clearance was lower, not higher, during sleep and anaesthesia. 354,467

Small human studies

What people show

One night without sleep (7 people against 17 controls) slowed clearance of a tracer from most brain regions. Sleep deprivation raised spinal-fluid amyloid by 25–30%, but mainly through more production, not less clearance. 129,330

Where this leaves it

That sleep affects amyloid levels is better supported than any specific glymphatic mechanism in human Alzheimer's. That is a synthesis across the studies above, not any single study's conclusion. Meningeal lymphatic vessels, described in 2015, may be another drainage route; their role in humans is unknown. 330,467,475

In plain wordsPoor sleep and amyloid are linked. How the brain "washes" itself at night is still argued about, mostly from mouse studies.

Part 1 · The disease

Genes and inheritance

Most Alzheimer's is not inherited in a simple way. One common gene, APOE, shifts the odds. A few rare genes all but guarantee it, and an extra chromosome 21 does too. Pick a genotype, then play the family below.

APOE: one gene, three common versions

Everyone carries two copies of APOE, one from each parent. The three common versions, ε2, ε3 and ε4, differ at only two positions in the protein (112 and 158). 531 Choose a pair to see how often it turns up in people with Alzheimer's compared with ε3/ε3.

Genotype

Odds ratios compare the odds of Alzheimer's with ε3/ε3, on a log scale. They are group averages, not anyone's personal chance.

Odds ratio is not lifetime risk, and the estimates disagree

An odds ratio of 15 does not mean a 15-times or a near-certain chance. Researchers have turned the odds into lifetime risk two ways, and get different answers. Rows for your chosen genotype are highlighted.

Why they disagree. Case-control and memory-clinic samples carry referral bias; the population cohorts measured MCI or dementia rather than Alzheimer's alone; and most cohorts are of European ancestry, where the ε4 effect is larger than in African ancestry. 21,47,420

What both agree on. ε4 raises risk but does not decide it: many ε4/ε4 people never develop dementia, and Alzheimer's often occurs without ε4. Only 38% of APOE alleles in people with Alzheimer's are ε4. 194,420,531

Dominant inheritance: APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2

A mutation in APP, PSEN1 or PSEN2, or an extra copy of APP, is the only known cause that all but guarantees Alzheimer's. 40 Pick the gene, play the family, and press "Another family" to see that 50% is a chance for each child, not a quota.

Gene

Schematic family. DIAN years are cross-sectional estimates relative to the parent's age at onset.

Down syndrome: a third copy of APP

APP, the gene for the protein amyloid beta is cut from, sits on chromosome 21. People with Down syndrome usually have three copies of chromosome 21, so three copies of APP. Drag the age, then switch to the rare case with only two APP copies.

Chromosome 21

Ages are from separate cohorts; positions on the ladder are to scale.

Resilience, risk scores and testing

Case reports + cohort

APOE3 Christchurch

A woman with the Colombian PSEN1 E280A mutation did not develop MCI until her seventies, about three decades late. She had two copies of APOE3 Christchurch, very high amyloid, and little tau. Among 1,077 carriers, the 27 with one Christchurch copy began to decline at a median 52 years against 47, about 5 years later. 26,421

Single case

RELN-COLBOS, 2023

A man with the same PSEN1 mutation stayed cognitively intact until 67 without Christchurch. He carried a gain-of-function variant in Reelin, which binds the same receptors as APOE; in mice it reduced tau phosphorylation. Both resilient people had very high amyloid but little entorhinal tau, suggesting protection acted at the tau stage. 26,323

Established

A673T: protection in APP itself

An Icelandic APP variant next to the beta-secretase site cut amyloid production by about 40% in the lab, and protected against Alzheimer's and against decline in older people without it. 262 See Amyloid, animated.

Established

The Colombian kindred

A 1997 survey of five extended families in Antioquia (nearly 3,000 people) found 128 affected, with onset at a mean 46.8 years. PSEN1 E280A traces to one founder about 15 generations ago. In 449 carriers, median ages were 44 for MCI, 49 for dementia and 59 for death. 8,296,322

Established

GWAS: 75 places in the genome

The largest study, Bellenguez 2022 in Nature Genetics (111,326 cases, 677,663 controls), found 75 risk loci, 42 new, pointing to amyloid and tau processing, microglia and TNF-α signalling. Rare TREM2 R47H raised risk about 2.9-fold. 46,263

Limited use

Polygenic scores

A score built with APOE, age and sex reached an AUC of 78.2%. Beyond age and APOE ε4, the Bellenguez score separated the top and bottom tenths by only 1.6- to 1.9-fold. Scores discriminate poorly in the general population, work less well outside European ancestry, and have no established clinical use. 46,144,309

Established

Twins: heritability 58–79%

In 11,884 Swedish twin pairs, heritability of Alzheimer's was 58% in the full model and 79% in the best-fitting one; the rest came from non-shared environment. Identical twins also differed less in age at onset. The authors stress non-genetic factors still matter. 190

Debated

Is ε4/ε4 its own genetic form?

In 2024, Fortea and colleagues reported Alzheimer's biology in almost all ε4/ε4 people, with symptoms at a mean of 65, and proposed it as a distinct genetic form. Critics answer that near-full penetrance of biology is not near-full penetrance of dementia, citing lifetime risks of about 30–55%. 21,184

Testing: what the guidelines say

Published guidance

Predictive APOE testing

A 1995 ACMG/ASHG statement said APOE should not be used for predictive testing. The 2011 ACMG/NSGC guideline calls APOE susceptibility testing "not clinically recommended" and advises against direct-to-consumer testing; if a person still insists after counselling, it says testing should follow the Huntington disease protocol. 7,201,202

Published guidance

Families with a dominant gene

The guideline says testing for APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2 should be offered to people with early-onset Alzheimer's and a family history, to families with a dominant pattern, and to relatives of a known carrier, using a Huntington-style protocol. Children should not be tested. Only 8.4% of at-risk people in one series asked for predictive testing. 40,201

Treatment context

Genotyping before anti-amyloid drugs

US labels for lecanemab and donanemab say ApoE ε4 testing "should be performed prior to initiation of treatment", because ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding on MRI) is more common in ε4/ε4. This is a different purpose from predicting Alzheimer's. 103,154,155,423 See Anti-amyloid antibodies.

Trial evidence

What disclosure did: REVEAL

162 adult children of people with Alzheimer's were randomised to learn their APOE result or not. At 1 year anxiety, depression and distress did not differ. ε4-positive people more often changed health behaviours (adjusted OR 2.73) and were 5.76 times more likely to change long-term care insurance. 72,208,539

Part 2 · Course and diagnosis

Twenty years before symptoms

Alzheimer's changes in the brain long before anyone notices. Biomarkers turn abnormal in a broadly predictable order: amyloid, then tau and nerve-cell damage, then thinking. Play the clock, and switch between families with a dominant gene and the common late-onset form.

Timeline

Where is this person on the 2024 map?

In 2024 an Alzheimer's Association workgroup proposed two scales: a biological stage from biomarkers (A to D, by how far tau has spread on PET) and a clinical stage from symptoms (0 to 6). The International Working Group (IWG) disagreed about what to call people without symptoms. Set the biomarkers and symptoms, or pick an example. 122,255

Examples
Amyloid (Core 1)
Tau PET
Symptoms

Shaded cells: the expected diagonal from 1A to 4–6D. Hatched: no Core 1 biomarker abnormal.

How the model and the definitions changed

Hypothetical model

Jack 2010, revised 2013

The 2010 model put amyloid first and neurodegeneration (CSF tau, MRI atrophy, FDG) after a variable lag, tracking symptoms. The 2013 update indexed people by time, added person-to-person variation, reordered some markers, and proposed that tau may start on its own in sporadic disease and be accelerated by amyloid. 252,253

Measured

DIAN, and its caveats

DIAN's numbers come from 128 mutation carriers placed on a clock set by the parent's age at onset. Longitudinal data from 217 people confirmed amyloid changes first, but disagreed with the cross-sectional timing of CSF tau by more than 10 years and showed CSF p-tau181 falling near onset. The authors warn the results may not apply to sporadic Alzheimer's. 41,345

Definitions moved

2011, 2018, 2024

In 2011, diagnosis was clinical and biomarkers were not advised for routine use. In 2018, a research framework defined Alzheimer's biologically and required A+ and T+. In 2024, one abnormal Core 1 result, such as amyloid alone, is enough. 254,255,347

Modelled

How long each phase lasts

Across 6 cohorts (3,268 people), someone with preclinical Alzheimer's at age 70 was estimated to spend about 10 years preclinical, 4 with MCI and 6 with dementia. Total duration ranged from 24 years starting at 60 to 15 years starting at 80. 501

Exam hookAmyloid is necessary for the biological label but tracks symptoms poorly; neurodegeneration tracks symptom severity, and tau stage carries prognosis. In cognitively unimpaired people, against A−T−, the hazard ratio for progressing to dementia was 1.5 for stage A, 5.6 for medial temporal tau and 39.9 for neocortical tau. 252,255

Part 2 · Course and diagnosis

Stages and symptoms

Alzheimer's takes away abilities in a fairly fixed order, from the most demanding tasks to the most basic ones. Press Play, or pick a stage, and watch which everyday abilities are kept and which are lost.

Schematic. Stages are drawn equal width, not to time. The year spans above come from one model (Vermunt 2019, someone with preclinical Alzheimer's at age 70). Reisberg's own average durations for each FAST stage are widely repeated but could not be checked against the 1988 paper (unverified), so they are not shown. CDR and MMSE are aligned to FAST approximately: the scales were built separately.

After a diagnosis of MCI: who progresses?

Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) means thinking has declined more than expected for age while daily life is still independent. It is a risk state, not a sentence. Two groups of 100 people with MCI are followed for five years below.

Illustration. Hollow figure: no dementia yet. Solid figure: progressed to dementia. It applies each published annual rate to those not yet converted, every year, which is a simplification: real risk differs from person to person.

Not always memory first

Typical Alzheimer's starts with memory, because the first tangles form in the medial temporal lobe. Some people start with vision, language or planning instead. These atypical forms are much more common when the illness starts before 65. 206

Each square is one person in 100. "About one third" is drawn as 33.

Beyond memory: mood and behaviour

Study

Pooled prevalence in Alzheimer's, Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Studies varied a lot.

How long, and how the illness ends

Established

Survival is measured in years

People aged 65 and older live on average 4 to 8 years after a diagnosis of Alzheimer's dementia, and some live as long as 20 years. Across studies, median survival from onset was 3.3 to 11.7 years, most often 7 to 10. 2,487

Established

Age at diagnosis matters most

Median survival was 8.3 years when diagnosed at 65 and 3.4 years at 90, with no significant difference between men and women. Across studies, age was a consistent predictor of death; male sex was a less consistent one. 64,487

Established

Pneumonia is the most common final event

Pneumonia is the most commonly identified immediate cause of death, and swallowing problems can lead to aspiration. In one autopsy series, respiratory causes accounted for 55.5% of deaths in Alzheimer's. 2,65

Advanced dementia in nursing homes

In the CASCADE study of 323 residents with advanced dementia, 54.8% died over 18 months. Eating problems affected 85.8% and pneumonia 41.1%. See Living with dementia for planning and end-of-life care. 358

Part 2 · Course and diagnosis

Diagnosis and biomarkers

A diagnosis is built in layers: first whether thinking has declined, then what else could explain it, then whether Alzheimer's pathology is present. Follow one person through the pathway, or click any step.

Schematic. Real pathways vary: not everyone needs every step, and the order can change. Each box can be clicked or reached with the Tab key.

What a positive blood test really means

Teaching tool This calculator shows arithmetic, not the performance of any real test in any real person. Pick how good a test is (sensitivity and specificity) and how likely the pathology is before testing. The grid then sorts 1,000 people by their true status and their result.

Test
Setting

Test presets: the 2025 Alzheimer's Association guideline minimums for a blood test used for triage (90% sensitivity, 75% specificity) or as a substitute for PET or CSF (90% and 90%) 399, and amyloid PET visual reads against autopsy 79. Settings: amyloid positivity in cognitively normal people at 50 256; a primary-care example value (no source here gives one measured figure); 50% with Alzheimer's pathology among 1,213 Swedish patients 398; amyloid PET positivity in IDEAS, among Medicare patients with MCI or dementia of uncertain cause 422.

Filled circle: true positive. Ring: false negative. Square: false positive. Small dot: true negative. Teaching tool, not a diagnostic calculator.

The biomarker toolbox

Established

Amyloid PET

Florbetapir visual reads found moderate-to-frequent neuritic plaques with 92% sensitivity and 100% specificity against autopsy within 2 years. The Centiloid scale runs from 0 (young controls) to 100 (typical mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's); about 12 to 24 Centiloids marked plaque thresholds at autopsy. 79,282,294

Established

Spinal fluid (CSF)

In Alzheimer's, CSF total tau is about 2.5 times and p-tau about 1.9 times control levels, and Aβ42 is about half. The Aβ42/40 ratio classifies better than Aβ42 alone. The FDA permitted the Lumipulse CSF ratio test in May 2022. 149,221,391

Established

Blood p-tau217

Plasma p-tau217 separated clinical Alzheimer's from other neurodegenerative diseases with AUC 0.96. In 1,213 Swedish patients, a p-tau217 test was about 90% accurate, against 61% for primary care doctors and 73% for specialists using standard workup. In May 2025 the FDA cleared the first blood test, for specialised care, "not intended as a screening or stand-alone diagnostic test". 153,397,398

Early evidence

A rule-out test for primary care

In October 2025 the FDA cleared Roche's Elecsys pTau181 plasma test for primary care, to help rule out Alzheimer's amyloid pathology. Its reported negative predictive value was 97.9%, a figure that depends on the low prevalence of the people studied. 433

Established

Tau PET and FDG-PET

Flortaucipir tau PET separated Alzheimer's from other neurodegenerative disorders with about 90% sensitivity and specificity, outperforming MRI volumes. FDG-PET patterns correctly classified 95% of Alzheimer's, 92% of Lewy body and 94% of frontotemporal dementia in a 7-centre study. 370,394

Not specific

NfL and GFAP

Neurofilament light rises with neurodegeneration of any cause, including MS, ALS and brain injury. GFAP, an astrocyte marker, rises with amyloid even before symptoms. The 2024 criteria use neither for diagnosis. 255,337,402

Screening tests: what they can and cannot do

MMSE

  • 11 items, 30 points; about 7 minutes. 59,94
  • At a cut-point of 24 in community settings: sensitivity 0.85, specificity 0.90 for dementia. 94
  • Strongly affected by schooling: median 29 with 9 or more years, 22 with 0 to 4 years. 95
  • Highly verbal and insensitive to mild impairment. 488
  • Under copyright; its authors began enforcing their rights in 2000, and licensed forms cost about USD 1.23 each in 2011. 380

MoCA

  • About 10 minutes, 30 points; adds executive and visuospatial tasks. In the original study a cut-off of 26 caught 90% of MCI, against 18% for the MMSE; specificity was 87%, against 100% for the MMSE. 374
  • The cut-off dispute: the owner keeps 26 or above as normal, with 1 point added for 12 or fewer years of education. A meta-analysis found 26 gives too many false positives, especially in older or less educated people, and the best accuracy at 23. 69,360
  • 2025 change: since December 2025, certification is optional for total-score screening but still required to interpret sub-scores. 360

Mini-Cog

  • Three-word recall (0 to 3) plus a clock drawing (0 or 2), total 0 to 5. A score of 0 to 2 means a higher likelihood of important impairment; a normal score does not rule it out. 355
  • About 3 minutes, and its accuracy was not affected by education or language in the original multilingual study. 59
  • In a meta-analysis: sensitivity 0.91, specificity 0.86 for dementia. 490
Established

The limit they share

Screening tools grade severity and prompt further assessment. They do not establish the cause. A highly educated person with early disease can score normally; low education, poor hearing or vision, or a language barrier can lower a score without dementia. 94,95,355,488

Exam hookMoCA for MCI, MMSE for grading dementia, Mini-Cog for speed. None of them names the cause.

Four definitions of Alzheimer's

The criteria have moved from a clinical syndrome toward biology, and the field disagrees about how far to go. Pick a person and see how each framework would label them.

Person

Part 2 · Course and diagnosis

The differential

Not every memory problem is Alzheimer's. How fast it started and what came first are among the strongest clues. Watch eight typical courses unfold on the same clock, then click any row for details.

Time axis

Typical patterns, schematic: higher line means better function. Solid line: thinking. Dashed line: the domain that leads (behaviour, gait or mood). Real people rarely follow a textbook course, and mixed causes are common.

The differential, condition by condition

Click a condition to open what else the sources say about it.

ConditionWhat points to it rather than Alzheimer'sKey tests and findings

Delirium or dementia?

Delirium is a medical emergency that can look like dementia, and it often happens on top of dementia. The Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) asks four questions. Switch the features on and off to see how the algorithm combines them.

Features present

Teaching illustration of the published algorithm, not a bedside tool. 248

FeatureDeliriumTypical Alzheimer's dementia
OnsetAcute: hours to days (CAM feature 1). 248Insidious, over months to years. 347
CourseFluctuates, often within a day. 248A clear history of gradual worsening. 347
First domainInattention, a required CAM feature. 248Usually recent memory. 2,206
ArousalLevel of consciousness may be altered (CAM feature 4). 248Dementia criteria require that delirium does not explain the symptoms. 347
ToolsCAM: under 5 minutes, 94 to 100% sensitivity and 90 to 95% specificity in validation. In people with dementia, one study found only 77% sensitivity. 248,367History from an informant, cognitive testing, then the workup in Diagnosis and biomarkers. 30
OverlapDelirium on top of dementia was reported in 22 to 89% of older people with dementia and linked to faster decline, institutional care and death. Fluctuating attention and arousal are also core features of Lewy body dementia. 171,346

The reversible-causes workup

Rates from a 2003 meta-analysis of 39 studies (5,620 people), scaled to 1,000 people. Positions are random.

Published guidance

Routine in the AAN parameter

Screening for depression, B12 deficiency and hypothyroidism, and a non-contrast CT or MRI, in the initial evaluation. This is a 2001 guideline. 284

Only when suspected

Syphilis serology when neurosyphilis is suspected. CSF or genetic testing is considered for atypical cases: onset before 65, rapid onset, or non-memory presentations. 30,284

Medicines

A medication review. The heaviest cumulative use of strong anticholinergics, most commonly tricyclic antidepressants, first-generation antihistamines and bladder antimuscarinics, was associated with dementia (hazard ratio 1.54). 207

Sleep

Sleep-disordered breathing was associated with incident MCI or dementia in 298 older women (odds ratio 1.85), following low oxygen rather than broken sleep. 530

Gait first

When walking changes first, imaging looks for the enlarged ventricles and DESH pattern of normal-pressure hydrocephalus; a CSF tap test may follow. 373

A sudden change

A sudden worsening points to delirium and a search for medical and drug causes, even in someone already living with dementia. 171,248

Part 3 · Treatment

Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine

The older Alzheimer's drugs act on the synapse, the gap where one neuron signals the next. Watch one cholinergic signal from start to finish, then switch to Alzheimer's or to a drug and play it again.

Show

Schematic, not to scale. The chart counts the molecules in the drawing; it is not measured data.

Memantine at the NMDA receptor

Memantine works on a different system: the NMDA receptor, a calcium channel opened by the transmitter glutamate. The idea behind it is to quiet a constant low-level leak through the channel while still letting a real signal through.

Blocker

Schematic. The channel has four subunits in reality; two are drawn. Traces are illustrative, not recordings.

Reading the evidence

Part 3 · Treatment

Anti-amyloid antibodies over time

Lecanemab and donanemab are antibodies infused into the blood that help the brain's immune cells clear amyloid plaque. Follow the published trials month by month: plaque falls fast, ARIA (brain swelling or small bleeds on MRI) shows up early, and the clinical benefit appears slowly and stays modest.

Published trial and label information only. Everything here reports what the trials, labels and regulators published. Whether a particular person is eligible, and whether treatment is right for them, are decisions for specialist clinicians together with the person and their family.

Part 4 · Living, caring, preventing

Lowering the risk

The 2024 Lancet Commission estimated how much dementia worldwide is linked to 14 risk factors that could, in principle, be changed. Play the wheel to build up its estimate, then pick any factor to see the evidence behind it and the caveats.

Population attributable fractions from the Commission's Figure 9, rounded to whole numbers. Click a segment or a row, or use the buttons below.

What the prevention trials found

A risk factor linked to dementia in observational studies is not proof that changing it prevents dementia. Randomised trials test that. Play the plot to bring in each trial's main result; many are null or small.

Dots are estimates; lines are 95% confidence intervals. A line that crosses the dashed no-effect line means the result is compatible with no effect. Units differ between rows, so compare each with its own zero.

The family carer

Words matter

Dementia Australia's language guidelines ask writers to put the person first. The table shows some of the swaps they suggest. 112

Stigma is common. In a global survey of almost 70,000 people, 62% of healthcare practitioners thought dementia is a normal part of ageing, 35% of carers had hidden a relative's diagnosis from at least one person, and over 85% of people living with dementia said their opinion had not been taken seriously. 9

Where sources disagree. The guidelines advise against "carer burden", preferring neutral wording such as "the impact of supporting someone". Research still measures "caregiver burden", for example with the Zarit Burden Interview used in trials. This page uses "impact" in its own words and "burden" only when naming a research measure. 112,189,297

Part 4 · Living, caring, preventing

Nursing care

Four parts of nursing care for a person living with dementia: assessment, giving the medicines, communication and care approaches, and documentation and safety. Each part has an animation or a tool to try, and each claim links to its source.

ScopeThis module describes what guidelines, drug labels and published studies say. It is not a care plan. It does not replace local protocols, your scope of practice, or the prescriber. Where the sources say no dementia-specific evidence exists, the module says so instead of filling the gap.

1 · Assessment

Delirium on top of dementia, hour by hour

Dementia changes over months and years. Delirium changes over hours and comes and goes. When the two overlap, the sudden change can hide inside the slow one. Press play to watch two weeks pass.

Delirium type Overlay

Teaching tool: a schematic curve, not data from any patient.

The 4AT, scored

Teaching tool, not a clinical record

Accuracy: a 2021 meta-analysis (17 studies, 3,702 observations) found pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.88 each. 486 In 785 acute medical patients aged 70 or over, the 4AT had sensitivity 76% and specificity 94%, while the CAM used in routine conditions had 40% and 100%. 459

Guidelines differ NICE CG103 (2023 update) names the 4AT when indicators of delirium are present, and the CAM-ICU or ICDSC in critical care. 384 NICE NG97 (2018) suggests the long CAM or the Observational Scale of Level of Arousal for inpatients with cognitive impairment of unknown cause, says instruments alone should not separate delirium from delirium on dementia, and says that when the two cannot be told apart, delirium is treated first. 383 A 2012 review found only 9 studies, with 50 participants who had delirium on dementia, validating any delirium tool in people with dementia. 367

4 · Documentation and safety

Build an ABC chart entry

An ABC chart records the Antecedent (what came just before), the Behaviour (described as seen and heard) and the Consequence (what happened next). Over many entries, a pattern can point to a need. Choose one of each to assemble a worked entry. The example is fictional.

A Cochrane review of 18 trials found that programmes built on functional analysis, of which ABC recording is the basis, reduced how often challenging behaviour happened and improved caregivers' reactions after the intervention, but not at follow-up. The analysis part could not be separated from the rest of each programme. No study was found that validates the ABC chart itself as a nursing documentation tool in dementia. 364

    Part 5 · Context and review

    History and people

    From one woman in a Frankfurt asylum in 1901 to the antibodies approved in 2023 and 2024. Scrub the timeline or press play: each era is drawn as a scene, with the milestone and its source in the panel beside it.

    Scenes are illustrations, not historical images. Eras are spaced evenly, not to scale in years. A "via a later review" label means the original paper has no abstract and its content comes through a later history review or Alzforum.

    What the history leaves open

    Debated

    Why a separate disease?

    Historians still debate why Kraepelin made a new disease from so few cases; one explanation is the rivalry between the Munich and Prague schools. The line between "presenile" Alzheimer's and "senile dementia" was dropped in 1978. 49

    Debated

    The amyloid cascade, three decades on

    Hardy and Higgins proposed the amyloid cascade hypothesis in 1992. A 2024 history review notes that the dominant amyloid hypothesis has so far yielded "poor therapeutic results". 49,222 See Amyloid, animated for the evidence on both sides.

    Now established

    Mixed causes in the oldest old

    The same 2024 review concludes that mixed dementia, with Alzheimer's changes alongside other brain diseases, is now established as the most frequent cause of dementia in the oldest old. 49

    Sources disagree

    How old was Auguste D.?

    One account gives her age as 50 when her symptoms began in 1901; another says she was 56 when she died in 1906. The sources disagree slightly. 49,235

      Alzheimer's Companion is an educational synthesis of the published literature on Alzheimer's disease, made for health-science students, people living with the disease, and the families who care for them.

      It is not medical advice. It cannot diagnose, and nothing here should change a treatment without your own clinician. Guideline doses are quoted as published. Please check the original sources, which are listed in full in the Sources module.
